Hey, I'm Edward Omondi, Software Engineer

I design, build and ship production platforms end to end: government case-management systems, mall loyalty programmes, carrier-grade SMS, lending and POS systems, and my own SaaS products. Based in Nairobi.
What I build, how I work, and how to work with me.
What technologies do you specialise in?

On the backend I work in Java with Spring Boot and Jakarta EE (WildFly), on PostgreSQL, with ActiveMQ Artemis for event-driven work and Keycloak for identity. My frontends are built in Nuxt (Vue) and Angular, and I build native Android apps in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose. I've integrated M-Pesa Daraja, Paystack, Stripe, KCB and Twilio, and I deploy to Linux servers on DigitalOcean with Apache, systemd and CI/CD.
Do you design full system architectures?

Yes. On my own products, Cardly, Kwaru and Ahadi, I own the whole architecture: modular Spring Boot backends, single-endpoint intent routing, Keycloak realms and roles generated from the API, idempotent payment webhooks, and multi-tenant data models. On client platforms I design the frontend architecture, for example one Nuxt codebase that serves four separately authenticated portals.
Have you worked with IoT or hardware integrations?

Yes. My BSc is in Mechatronics Engineering. For Aims I built a Raspberry Pi controller in Python that drives solenoid smart locks for short-term rental units, connected to a Spring Boot API. I also built an RFID wearable-based points-tracking system for an entertainment venue.
What scale of projects have you worked on?

They range from national government systems to solo SaaS products. They include a non-tariff-barrier reporting and case-management system for South Africa's trade department, a loyalty and e-purse platform for a major Nairobi mall, a regulatory licensing portal for a national food and drug authority, a carrier-grade SMS platform delivering across Kenya's three mobile networks, and several SaaS products I built and run myself.
What does your delivery process look like?

I write the spec and the key design decisions down before building. I then ship in small, deployable phases with lint, type checks and tests in CI, and deploy with scripts that roll back automatically if a health check fails. Identity, payments and audit logging are designed in from the start, not bolted on later.
Are you available for consulting or contracts?
Yes. I take on contract roles, technical consulting and end-to-end product builds, remotely or in Nairobi. Email me at ewomondi@gmail.com with a short description of the project.
How does your engineering background shape your work?

I hold a BSc in Mechatronics Engineering from JKUAT (Second Class Honours, Upper Division). Training across electrical, mechanical and software systems taught me to think about the whole system. That habit carries over to software: I trace a problem from the user's screen down to the queue, the database or the device.
Do you have training in security?

Yes. I'm a Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH, EC-Council) and hold Cisco's Introduction to Cyber Security certificate. In practice, that shows up in Keycloak hardening, signed and IP-whitelisted APIs, HMAC-verified webhooks, and encrypting secrets at rest.

After years of building Spring Boot APIs for production systems — from gift card platforms to IoT-connected web applications — I've developed patterns that consistently produce clean, maintainable, and scalable REST services. Here's what I've learned.

. Controllers handle HTTP concerns only. Services contain business logic. Repositories abstract data access. Mixing these creates code that's impossible to test or maintain at scale.

State management is where many Angular projects become unnecessarily complex. After building several production Angular applications — including the Aims property management system and Herdwise — here's the approach I've settled on.
For most application state, a well-designed service with
observables is all you need. Components subscribe to the stream, the service manages transitions — no store libraries required.

Angular's built-in signals are now my first choice for component-level and simple shared state. They're synchronous, fine-grained, and require zero boilerplate:

Only introduce a state management library if you genuinely need time-travel debugging, complex cross-module state sharing, or a very large team that benefits from strict conventions. For most projects I've worked on — including Aims and Herdwise — that bar is never reached.
The real win is keeping your components thin. Push logic into services, keep templates declarative, and your application stays testable and understandable even as it grows.

Keep it simple. Reach for complexity only when simple provably breaks.

Authentication is one of those things you really don't want to get wrong. After implementing Keycloak across multiple production systems at Technovation Ventures, I've developed a reliable pattern for integrating it with Spring Boot backends and Angular frontends.

Keycloak gives you a full OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect identity provider you can self-host. You get user management, social logins, MFA, and fine-grained authorisation — without building any of it yourself. For B2B SaaS or multi-tenant systems, it's hard to beat.
